expect/two: A model answers two questions, eight times each. A checker gives each answer a reward, r: one if it is right, zero if it is wrong.
expect/news: Seven times eight is easy for it: seven of its eight answers are right. Seventeen times twenty four is hard: just one is.
expect/worth: A right answer to the hard one is news, worth a big push. On the easy one, it is what the model does anyway.
expect/same: A baseline is the reward you expected. One baseline shared by every question would push those two alike, so each question needs its own.
expect/value: One way is to train a second network to predict it: a value model, since a question's value is the reward it is expected to bring.
expect/cost: In 2024, Zhihong Shao and colleagues at DeepSeek pointed out the cost: that network is usually about as big as the model itself.
expect/group: Their way needs no second network: the mean reward of the question's own group of answers is its baseline. Seven eighths here, one eighth there.
expect/name: They called it GRPO, for group relative policy optimization. It improves the policy, the model's rule for answering, by judging each answer relative to its own group.
curve/r: Now one question, with a group of G answers. The DeepSeek Math paper sampled sixty four; here there are eight, and three are right.
curve/mean: Their mean reward is three eighths, zero point three seven five. Draw it as a level line through the rewards: the baseline.
curve/right: Subtract it, as with any baseline. Right answers sit zero point six two five above the line, and wrong ones zero point three seven five below.
curve/spread: How spread out is the group? Square each distance from the line, average the squares, and take the square root: the standard deviation, a typical distance from the mean.
curve/std: Here it is about zero point four eight four. Shade a band that far on either side of the line.
curve/dright: Divide by it, to count each distance in standard deviations. A right answer: zero point six two five over zero point four eight four, about one point two nine.
curve/dwrong: A wrong one: minus zero point three seven five over zero point four eight four, about minus zero point seven seven.
curve/A: That is GRPO's advantage, A: each reward, minus the group's mean, over the group's standard deviation.
curve/curve: It is grading on a curve, each answer marked against its own group, so the scale of the rewards drops out: pay ten for a right answer instead of one, and every advantage stays the same.
agree/hard: Back to the hard question: mean one eighth, standard deviation about zero point three three. Its one right answer gets about two point six five, a big push.
agree/easy: On the easy one, each right answer gets only about zero point three eight, and the wrong one about minus two point six five.
agree/all: If every answer is right, each reward equals the mean, and every advantage is zero: the group teaches nothing. All wrong, the same.
agree/eps: The standard deviation is zero then, so code adds a tiny number to it, and zero divided by that stays zero.
agree/sum: In every group, the advantages add up to zero: probability moves from the worse answers to the better ones.
agree/cost: So GRPO trains no value model. Its price is a whole group of answers for every question.
